title: Upgrade Execution Safety Playbook and Lightweight E2E Prober
creator: Asha Patel
description: Define an executable safety playbook and lightweight end-to-end prober for release preflight that combines smoke checks, targeted perf-regression gates, and behavioral evals tuned for LTS and non-LTS channels. The goal is to reduce release rollbacks and undetected regressions while keeping preflight time under 30 minutes for quick patch releases.
background: We currently run a suite of heavy synthetic workloads and long-running perf jobs for major releases. Smaller patch releases and frequent commits lack a fast, deterministic preflight that exercises routing, KV cache warming, basic model fidelity checks, and latency SLOs across Dedicated and Hosted. This causes noisy rollouts and occasional customer impact. We need a compact, reproducible prober + playbook that can be run automatically in CI and manually by SRE during emergency upgrades.
proposed_solution: 1) Implement a lightweight E2E prober (go binary + container) that runs a prioritized set of checks: connectivity, model load + KV warmup, 95th percentile token latency, generation correctness smoke tests (structured output sanity), and simple regression anchors (signature metrics). 2) Add policy-driven gates: fail-fast for >5% latency regression or >2% fidelity drop on smoke prompts. 3) Integrate results into the release orchestration service (release-api) with pass/fail artifact and links to artifacts. 4) Ship a one-page ‘Upgrade Safety Playbook’ runbook that guides operators through triage and rollback actions when prober fails.
acceptance_criteria: Lightweight prober runs end-to-end in <= 30 minutes on a standard preflight runner image
Automated gate enforcement in release pipeline: patch releases blocked if prober fails
Perf regression detection: alerts when 95th percentile token latency deviates >5% from baseline
Fidelity anchors: structured-output smoke prompts show <2% regression in key metrics or trigger a block
Playbook contains clear rollback steps, canary trimming, and postmortem checklist
Dashboards display prober results per build and per model with historical deltas
rollout_strategy: Start with runtime-1.22 alpha channel for two weeks, then LTS candidate runs for the next scheduled maintenance window. For Dedicated customers, enable a graceful opt-in flag. Enforce gating on canary jobs for non-blocking experimentation before enabling for patch releases.
test_plan: Create containerized prober image and publish to internal registry
Add a CI job (preflight/light) that runs prober on PRs tagged 'release-candidate'
Run prober against three recent commits and record baseline metrics
Simulate controlled regressions (inject 10% added latency) to validate thresholds and alerts
Perform cross-channel validation: hosted, dedicated small pool, private-vpc sandbox
monitoring_and_alerting: Create prober-metrics dashboard in Grafana with time-series for token latency P50/P95/P99, error-rates, and fidelity score
PagerDuty policy: page on sustained 95th percentile regression >8% or fidelity drop >5% for >10 minutes
Slack release channel webhook posts per-run summary with pass/fail and links to artifacts
Retention: store prober run artifacts and traces for 90 days for regression analysis
rollout_playbook_steps: Step 1: Start preflight runner and execute prober (automated via release-api)
Step 2: If prober passes, continue with canary rollout (10% traffic) and run live-sanity checks
Step 3: If prober fails, capture artifacts, tag the build as 'blocked' and run lightweight bisect to narrow commmit range
Step 4: Escalate to on-call SRE + owning engineer if bisect points to recent change
Step 5: If immediate rollback required, trigger release-api rollback and notify customers per the communication template
Step 6: Post-incident: run extended perf harness and open a postmortem with action items
tradeoffs_and_risks: Tight thresholds reduce false negatives but increase false positives — may delay valid patches
Prober may miss long-tail regressions that only appear at scale; heavy synthetic jobs still required for major releases
Maintenance overhead: prober must be kept aligned with model changes and protocol updates
Dedicated/private topology variance could cause spurious failures; need topology-aware baselines
